maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-STATEMENT BY MINISTER

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so that the House may understand the Opportunities for Youth program more fully, I would like to take a few moments to outline detailed information about the program and to place it within the context of the over-all summer employment and activities programs of the federal government for this year.
As you know, the total budget for the summer 71 program is about $67.8 million, which represents the provision of more than 70,000 jobs. This compares with last year's spending of $33.2 million, which resulted in the creation of jobs for 38,300 young people. In certain respects, however, this is a misleading comparison because this year's programs emphasize to a much greater extent activities which do not provide direct employment. I am thinking here of the tens of thousands who are engaged this summer in language training programs, athletic endeavours or travelling. An important objective of the summer employment programs is to offset regional disparities by providing more assistance to those regions that are hardest hit by student unemployment. The number of students in each region and the levels of other provincial and federal spending in each region that would create summer jobs have been taken into consideration. Opportunities for Youth moneys has been carefully allocated to assist the government in achieving this balance. For instance, the following is a breakdown of
the Opportunities for Youth allocations by region: Atlantic Region, $2.8 million; Quebec, $9 million; Ontario, $5 million; Prairies and N.W.T., $3.8 million; B.C. and Yukon, $2.4 million; National, $.5 million.
Embarking on such an endeavour, we must be prepared to face certain problems. Not all of us have the same needs, nor do we often agree on the measures which should be taken to satisfy them. Nevertheless, I am confident that we can overcome the difficulties which will develop, although there already have been problems and there will likely be more before the summer is over. Some of the problems are administrative: it has not been possible to finalize project approvals as quickly as we had hoped; nor has it been possible to release the project funds as quickly as had been planned. But all in all there were some 13,000 project applications to process and we are at the present time dealing with 2,500 approved projects involving some 30,000 people.

I know that many students who responded to the Opportunities for Youth challenge have been disappointed and some of those who have had their projects approved have felt frustrated over some of the delays. But I also know that the vast majority have shown real understanding and appreciation of what is involved in implementing this program.
At the same time, the government recognizes and has recognized from the beginning its responsibility to Parliament and to the people for the spending of public funds on a program of this nature. This responsibility weighs more heavily in respect of a program that is admittedly experimental. To those who have voiced concern towards this aspect of the program, I would like to set out the four means by which the government will discharge its responsibilities for the spending of these moneys.
First, every Opportunities for Youth project will be visited by an official of my department. He will ensure that the project is carrying out the activities and fulfilling the objectives that were agreed to. No further payments will be made to projects that are carrying on activities other than those agreed in the government's contracts with the project organizers.
Second, all projects receiving funds in excess of $25,000 will receive an audit by the Department of Supply and Services. The department will also run spot audits of all other projects. In addition, all projects are required to submit financial statements before the final payment is made.
Third, an evaluation of the program will be carried out on which the young people themselves, community officials and voluntary organizations will contribute their views. In addition, a range of outside experts in community development, youth activities and social research will be asked to assist on this evaluation.
Fourth, the government undertakes to publish a report on this evaluation at the conclusion of the program. This report will be tabled in the House and made available to

June 18, 1971

participants in the Opportunities tor Youth program and the general public tor discussion and comment.
These steps are, of course, in addition to the careful examinations of projects made by my officials based on criteria agreed to by Treasury Board and explained on Wednesday by the Minister without Portfolio responsible for citizenship (Mr. Stanbury) and on other occasions by myself and other members of the government. They should provide the basis upon which this House can place its faith in the responsibility of our young people and, at the same time, feel confident that it is carrying out its responsibilities for the spending of public funds.
When we designed the Opportunities for Youth program, we knew it was experimental. We knew there would be problems of implementation. But we had confidence in the responsibility and good sense of young people. We still have that confidence and I certainly have seen nothing in the criticism that has emerged to date to shake that confidence. I have seen innuendo. I have seen unspecific and unsubstantiated sweeping attacks.
The attacks that have come are absolutely true to the tradition we have come to expect from critics of the young. They jump on isolated incidents and use them to pillory a whole generation. They scream about youth problems and disregard the overwhelming positive and constructive activity that the young embrace so enthusiastically, time and time again. They demand that we institutionalize and bureaucratize programs involving the young to the point where all possibility of error is eliminated.

Mr. Speaker, I do not entirely blame the minister for wanting to divert attention from many of the fundamental problems that exist within the Opportunities for Youth program. I suppose it is only natural that in his desire to avoid and deflect the obvious criticism from many sources he should try to mislead this House and the public badly. There has been evidence of that this morning.
There had been some hope that the minister, after so many weeks and months of engaging in this process, might have something worth while to contribute this morning. Indeed, it was announced well in advance that he would make a statement in the House today on the Opportunities for Youth program. He did not even have the courtesy to send a copy of his statement to the opposition parties before the sitting began. One would have thought that, rather than only a few words to those who submitted the close to 11,000 projects which have been rejected, he would have had more to say than:
But I also know that the vast majority have shown real understanding and appreciation of what is involved in implementing this program.
I am sure they know only too well, now that they have received the thousands of form letters which say next to nothing as to the reasons for which their programs have been rejected.
I think it is absolutely shocking that the minister should have the effrontery to come before the House today without being prepared to answer some of the specific questions which have been asked time and time again in this place. On Wednesday I reminded both the parliamentary secretary and the minister without portfolio in charge of winking that the minister had confirmed to me many weeks ago that there would be an active process of negotiation with regard to rejected projects with other authorities, whether they be municipal,

June 18, 1971
Opportunities for Youth Program
provincial, industrial, universities or other such groups that might be prepared to pick up projects that the government was not prepared to finance. I have yet to hear from the minister, from his parliamentary secretary or from the Minister without Portfolio any response to what is a basic question that thousands of our young people who in all sincerity submitted projects are expecting to be answered.
Why did these people receive nothing more than a form letter from the minister as of June 8, June 9 or whenever it was? Why has the minister not been prepared to tell us about the kind of consultation and negotiations that took place with regard to these programs? Why is the only response of the minister to say that they must surely understand what is involved in the implementation of the program?
We have asked as well why it is that this program was put together, as the minister himself has said, as a crash program. Why was the whole office for the Opportunities for Youth program assembled at such a late date? We are still waiting for a clear statement so that we can learn in a positive way from the unfortunate experiences of the administration of the program this year.
It is not enough for the minister to come here and to accuse indirectly members of the House, members of the press gallery or members of the general public of having no faith in our young people. I think our young people are asking how much interest this government has in them that it could put together at such a late date such a fuzzily defined program and then try to pass it off as the finet thing any government has done for Canadian youth. What utter nonsense, Mr. Speaker!
If the minister is seriously concerned about looking at the real issues that exist in the program, then let him examine the criteria. We have had a kind of tantalizing process in this regard. The minister has told us on the one hand that we have all the necessary criteria for the acceptance or rejection of projects, and then a little later somebody else comes along and adds some new information, new ideas, and these are tossed into the pot at the last moment.
We have been told that there are to be some specific auditing procedures, that there will be investigations made by representatives of the minister's department. I should like to ask in what way these investigations will be carried out. What criteria will the investigators use? What assurance have young people whose projects have already been accepted that their projects will not be terminated next week or the week after? The minister has not explained any aspects of these newly announced criteria.
With regard to administrative processes, if the minister wishes to operate with a clean hand surely he should be willing to allow a much fuller disclosure of the present procedures in regard to the Opportunities for Youth program. I suggest that it is in the minister's own best interests seriously to consider the establishment of a small all-party committee so that its members might look in detail at the administrative effectiveness of the program with a view to making recommendations regarding any program that might be operated in 1972.
I suggested earlier that in an over-all way what we needed was a special committee on youth to consider the impact of this program and other programs presently being operated by the government. There has been no response on that front either by the minister.
Once again the members of this House have been given a statement by the minister in which he has tried to deflect and diffuse accurate and honest criticisms of a program that at its inception could have had tremendous possibilities for the young people of this country. We are asking this government to please address itself to the facts and to stop fooling around as it has been to date.

Mr. Speaker, when the minister made the first announcement about this program it was just one month before university students would be finishing their courses and looking for the work they need if they are to earn the money to go back to university next fall. I pointed out at that time that the delay in working out the plans and announcing what the government intended to do till that late date was a criminal act on the part of the government which could not be defended. I predicted that a large number of young people would be disappointed and would not get work. I predicted that many of the projects which would be approved would not have the scrutiny required so that we would be assured the projects actually approved were the best ones. There are thousands of young people who hoped to get work but could not find it in the private sector of the economy and did not hear that they could not get work through these projects until the first of June. I hope the minister will tell them where they are going to earn the money so they can go back to school next fall, and not blame the opposition.
We asked the minister repeatedly what the criteria were and it was like pulling teeth to get an answer. What do we now find? One of the main criteria used by the people who are sifting through the many projects is that a project which is conceived and proposed by young people will have priority over other projects. The minister says that members of the opposition are not specific and that they are making innuendoes in the kind of complaints they put forward. I want to give the minister two examples from my own area which have come to my attention unsolicited.
The YMCA and B'Nai Brith are two organizations which have had probably a quarter of a century of experience in operating day care centres and day camps. They submitted proposals for that kind of project in Winnipeg. The projects they proposed would have employed only young people. They were planned by people who had had experience, but they were turned down.

maintopic: OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Shame!

I say when things are over we will find that the experience of this year will be as bad or worse than the experience we had with the Company of Young Canadians.
Let me talk about the future. The government has fumbled and bumbled and made a mess of this year's program. In 1972 young people will again be looking for jobs. I urge the minister and his department to work on plans for 1972 this fall. I urge the minister to have the plans ready and to make them public by December 31, 1971, so that next April or May we will not have a rush job with the same kind of rooting around to find projects in order to use up the money, much of which will be used in the wrong way as has been the case in 1971.

speechtext: I would like to direct a question to the Secretary of State. In view of the fact that the agreements between the federal government and the provinces for the financing of post-secondary education expire in 1972, and in light of the very serious consequences to post-secondary education and to the provinces if the agreements are not renewed or new agreements negotiated, would the minister consider making a statement before the House rises at the end of this month about the position of the federal government with regard to the future of the financing of post-secondary education?

speakerposition: Minister of Communications; Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON FINANCING OF POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION IN LIGHT OF EXPIRY OF AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES IN 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would quite willingly consider the proposal of the member. But I must point out to him that since January repeated and intensive negotiations have been held with
the Canadian Council of Ministers of Education, as well as bilateral negotiations with each of the provincial Ministers of Education-all very important people-since this is a field of provincial jurisdiction. We still hope to come to an agreement, which would allow a statement to be made to this House, not only on the attitude of the federal government, which is generally known, to the effect that an agreement has been renewed for two years, and that in the meantime plans will be made for a complete revision of the agreements in 1974. Obviously, however, for a general statement to be made, we should have completed our present negotiations with the provinces; unfortunately, this is not yet the case.

This is a matter of concern not only for the federal government, that foots 50 per cent of the bill, but for most provinces, that pay the remaining 50 per cent.

subtopic: PILOTAGE ACT

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-246, respecting pilotage, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subtopic: PILOTAGE ACT
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF PILOTAGE AUTHORITIES AS PROPRIETARY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
That Bill C-24S, respecting pilotage, be amended by adding to Clause 15 at page 13 immediately after subclause (7) the following:
" (8) A pilotage certificate shall be valid for use by the holder thereof only on ships of Canadian registry".
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendment I have proposed to this bill is not likely to receive widespread attention in the press, particularly in view of the events that are scheduled to take place later today. Before I get into the substance of my amendment, I would like to suggest that in these days when we are increasingly concerned about the ecological health of our country and the world, this legislation is very important to us all.
After having undergone one of the most strenuous committee sessions that I have ever attended, I remarked that this bill does not have very much political sex appeal. None the less, the work that was done in the standing committee on this bill was a very worthwhile exercise. We were dealing with a very complex piece of legislation on a subject which does not come to the
attention of Members of Parliament very often. We worked hard trying to understand the complexities of the bill and did what we could to improve it. This is indicated by the fact that a number of amendments were written into the original draft by the committee.
Those who were most concerned about the bill, particularly the pilots who were very assiduous in their attendances at the hearings, were by and large very happy with the results of the work of the committee. They expressed themselves quite freely in that context. However, it was unfortunate that, because of a rather irrelevant clause in this bill, irrelevant in the context of the total package which has to do with legislation due to expire June 30, the committee hearings were rushed and the pressures under which we worked were rather extreme for a bill of this complexity.
My assessment of what happened in the committee with regard to the total picture of what is proposed in the bill, is that there appears to be one defect that is worthy of consideration. For that reason, I placed this amendment on the order paper for discussion. The amendment reads:
A pilotage certificate shall be valid for use by the holder thereof only on ships of Canadian registry.
To put this amendment in context, it is necessary to appreciate the main purpose of the bill. It provides for a new concept of semi-autonomous regional pilotage authorities which will be responsible for most of the administrative work of the pilotage service in their respective regions. Clause 12 clearly states that the central purpose of the bill is to have the pilotage authorities operate an efficient pilotage service in the interests of safety. This is the over-riding consideration in the whole matter of having a pilotage service. It is central to consideration of my amendment and, indeed, almost any other proposal in the bill. It is with the object of raising certain questions as to the adequacy of the bill with regard to the matter of safety that I would like to discuss certain provisions of the bill at this stage.
The bill provides, and this is most important and certainly central to my amendment, that in effect there are to be two classes of people who will be empowered to have responsibility for piloting ships in the compulsory pilotage areas in Canadian waters which will be established under the bill. There are the people who are in our present pilotage service, the people we normally refer to as pilots. There is provision for granting pilotage certificates to officers of certain ships. I do not quarrel with this basic concept. It is not because of any quarrel with this proposal that I have introduced my amendment. I am sure the minister and, more particularly, his parliamentary secretary who sat in on the committee meetings, will recognize that a great deal of discussion in the committee centered around who should be the holders of pilotage certificates and under what circumstances.
Indeed, the committee did propose a number of amendments designed to clarify the question who should receive pilotage certificates. The committee wrote a provision into clause 14 that the holders of such certifi-
[Mr. Basford.l
June 18, 1971

cates would be required, as are pilots, to undergo further training and examination from time to time. This was a step toward keeping the qualifications of those who receive certificates on a par with those of regular pilots. Another amendment agreed to in committee was that the holder of a pilotage certificate must be a Canadian citizen or a landed immigrant, a stipulation being that the landed immigrant must become a Canadian citizen within five years if he wished to continue to hold his certificate.
We introduced an amendment to another clause designed to make it clear that the holder of a pilotage certificate must be qualified in navigational skills and possess a knowledge of the area in which he operates equivalent to that possessed by holders of a regular pilot's licence. I suppose it could be argued that with these additional safeguards the bill covers all the questions which needed to be dealt with. It is fair to say that most of the pilots felt we had gone a great distance toward ensuring that holders of pilotage certificates would, in fact, be people who possess qualifications similar to those of the pilots themselves.
There is another matter which is of considerable importance and it received a good deal of attention in committee, namely, the relationship between the master of a ship and the person responsible for performing the pilotage function. The bill seeks to clarify this relationship by virtue of a couple of amendments which were introduced in committee. It is spelled out for the first time in Canadian law, I believe, that a licensed pilot who has the conduct of a ship is responsible to the captain for the safe navigation of the vessel. This is provided by amendments to clause 16 to be found on page 13 of the bill. Later in the same clause hon. members will find an additional provision making it clear that the master has the authority, should he deem it necessary, to take over the control of the ship from the pilot at any time, though if he does so he must report his reasons for so doing to the pilotage authority.
When a pilot is aboard a ship it might be considered that there is a dual authority. This arises from the fact that the pilot is not responsible to the master as far as general directions are concerned; he is responsible to the agency which, in effect, is his employer, namely, the pilotage authority. So the pilot is placed in an independent position in his relationship to the master. Though in the last analysis he is under the control of the master while he is aboard, when he steps off the ship he is completely divorced from his relationship with that officer. This is not, however, the situation which will apply to those who hold pilotage certificates, people who may be second or third mates on a vessel. One of the requirements the committee wrote into the bill is that if a person is obliged to function as a navigational officer, as the holder of a pilotage certificate, he has to be a member of the complement of the ship's crew. So we have a man who is the holder of a pilotage certificate in a continuing relationship with the master of a vessel, under his general direction at all times, in addition to the particular relationship which exists while he is engaged in performing a pilot's function.
Pilotage Act
This is a feature of the situation about which we ought to be very careful because there is a good deal of concern in the minds of many of us that in these circumstances the member of the crew performing the pilotage function may not be in a position to exercise independent judgment in relation to what he does as a pilot. This is because he would be dependent for his job, for his career, on maintaining the good will of the master of the ship and, in addition, on being willing to work at all times under his direction. He would be in a position in which the master could exercise strong and continuing pressure upon him. While the holder of a pilotage certificate may have qualifications equivalent to those of a regular pilot, while he may have equivalent knowledge of the waters of the area in which he operates, it is open to question whether the interests of safety with respect to navigation will be as fully protected as would be the case were a fully qualified licensed pilot independent of the master, responsible for the navigation of the ship. There appears to be no question in the minds of pilots with whom I have discussed this question with regard to the situation in the coastal trade. They know that in most cases, under the arrangements envisaged by this bill, there should be no problem in having as master of a ship a person with knowledge of the waters and navigational skills that make for the safe navigation of his vessel.
Indeed, those of us who have had some experience living in seacoast areas know that in fact masters in our coasting trade have established a very good reputation and record in relation to the safe navigation of their vessels in some of the most difficult waters in the world over a long period of years. While there have been occasional accidents at sea and incidents of mis judgment that have caused disasters of one kind or another, in the total picture such events have been few and far between. With the continuing kind of action envisaged by the bill, and as a result of some of the amendments we made to the Canada Shipping Act, I think the record of the past can be improved upon in the future as far as our coasting trade is concerned.
The concern that was expressed to me following the committee's consideration of the bill, a concern which to my way of thinking is a legitimate and real one, is that, as the bill now stands, the practice could develop whereby we would have foreign line ships employing as a matter of deliberate policy second or third mates who are Canadians and holders of Canadian pilotage certificates. As the bill stands, if someone who is the holder of a pilotage certificate is a ship's officer, the vessel could be exempt from taking on a pilot in the compulsory pilotage waters of Canada.
I think this is a very different situation from that which prevails with respect to our coasting trade. Here, you will have a junior officer of a ship, at all times under the direction of a master, who has no local knowledge of Canadian waters; who may not even speak either one of our official languages; who is unfamiliar with many of the local customs in respect of navigation that are thor-

June 18, 1971
Pilotage Act
oughly understood by the pilots in our pilotage service, as well as by masters of coasting vessels who are travelling through these waters on a continuing, year-round basis. I think this is a situation that we should examine, and it is something on which my amendment tends to focus attention. I think it is obvious to hon. members that the effect of my amendment would be to provide that these pilotage certificates would be valid only on ships of Canadian registry.
I am not certain that the exact terms of my amendment fully and completely meet this situation. I might be willing to concede in our discussion that there may be some situations where it might be logical to agree that a pilotage certificate is valid on a foreign line vessel. But from such knowledge as I have, which as far as it goes is principally related to the Pacific coast, I think such situations should be few and far between.
I would further argue that while a person may have met all the qualifications required for holding a pilotage certificate, if he is in fact going to be employed on a non-Canadian vessel that is travelling the high seas and which only periodically visits areas along the coast of Canada where his pilotage certificate is valid, then inevitably he will lose his familiarity with the area, apart from anything else. For example, he will have to concern himself with duties that involve him in Hong Kong, Japan, Australia, the United Kingdom and other parts of the world. He will spend only a small part of his time in giving active attention to navigating a ship in Canadian coastal waters and approaching our ports. Most of the time his mind will be concentrating on other duties in other ports of the world, duties that are not directly related to the piloting of a ship in Canadian coastal waters.
In terms of safety, I suggest this is a matter that should be carefully examined. If my amendment can be better worded or in some way qualified in respect to its rather bald terms, then I for one would be prepared to listen to any suggestions and, with the agreement of the House, arrive at some different form of wording or at what might even be considered to be compromise wording. But with my limited knowledge, this is the best effort that I have been able to make by way of amendment and is what I thought would meet the basic requirements of what I am trying to achieve.
The emphasis and thrust of this amendment is directed at the main purpose of the bill, which is the operation of a safe, efficient pilotage service in the interest of general safety. Let me say at once that my discussions with pilots would lead me to believe it is not simply a question of their worrying about whether or not their individual jobs would be safeguarded. This issue is much broader than that. From my own experience of meeting some of the people engaged in the pilotage service on the Pacific coast-and I think there are some 80 of them-these people are a very high calibre of Canadian indeed. They are men of experience and judgment, and I think it is obvious on the face of it that this is what they should be. They are men whose whole focus on life is to ensure that ships can move safely in and out of our Canadian ports
and waters. They have a great deal of pride in their work, since they recognize that they exercise a responsibility in the matter of safety that no comparable group of Canadians in any other field exercises. Like many of the rest of us, they are aware of the increasing responsibilities they have to bear with the development of larger and larger ships carrying pollutant cargoes in larger and larger quantities.
They are aware, as very few other Canadians are, of the real danger of a major disaster at sea, particularly in coastal areas. If we do, as I suppose we must, accept the fact that bulk cargoes on the sea moving from our ports to foreign ports and from the ports of other countries to our ports are going to be carried in larger and larger vessels and that there are going to be more of them, we have to recognize how crucial and important some of these questions can be. Indeed, I readily say at once that the fact this bill was introduced by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) is an indication that the government recognizes such to be the case.
Quite frankly, one of the things I do not like about my amendment is that it might be argued it runs contrary to a principle with which I agree as enunciated by the minister's spokesman before the committee. Our concern should be primarily with the competence of the people on the bridge rather than with questions surrounding ownership or the flag of the vessel. This is essentially a sound principle, and my amendment or any other should be viewed in that context. The practical realities of the situation as I see them, and certainly this was in my mind and I think in the minds of most other members of the committee as we discussed the pros and cons of the situation, are that primarily pilotage certificates would go to ships' officers in our coasting trade, in whom we do have a pretty high degree of confidence because of the knowledge they possess and the constant and continuing experience they gain.
If the practice develops and becomes widespread of foreign lines deliberately employing Canadians as officers for the purpose of short-circuiting the kind of regulations which would force them to take independent pilots aboard, then I think there is a real fear some of the fundamental purposes of this bill will be circumvented. Hon. members of the House can realize that, up to a point at least, the owners and managers of shipping lines, who are thinking in terms of dollars and cents, are going to say why not avoid paying pilotage fees by having a qualified second or third mate on the vessel? This would make it possible for them to dispense with pilotage services. These pressures can build up.
In concluding my discussion on this amendment, perhaps I can do so best by telling the House of a situation which developed, a detail of which I only learned recently. It concerns the motor vessel Scheydyck which is now at the bottom of Nootka Sound in my constituency. At the time the Scheydyck had taken on its load of pulp from the Gold River Pulp Mills cargo dock. This was a new port and some of the navigational aids, lights and so

June 18, 1971

on, now in that Muchalat Inlet were not there and the judgment of the pilots at that time was that this was not a safe channel to navigate in the dark. One of our B.C. pilots felt so strongly that this was the case he would not take that ship, even though it would have been his normal turn to do so. However, another pilot did go with the view of trying to persuade the Master not to leave until dawn. He was overruled by the Master and the ship left port in the evening. Whether this was primarily the cause of the ship now being at the bottom, I do not know. I am not sure this can be determined because the vessel is down at the bottom of Nootka Sound and something may have gone wrong with the controls or equipment on the vessel.
The fact of the matter is that had there only been a second or third mate on that ship who was the holder of a licence certificate there could have been no argument about the ship sailing if the Master said it was to sail. This was one of the thoughts in my mind which led me to proposes my amendment to the bill. This is the kind of practical situation which can develop, because Masters responsible to their owners want to get their ships under way in order to be in another port at a certain time to finish taking on cargo, get back on the high seas and meet a loading schedule somewhere on the other side of the world. This is the attitude because it means dollars in the pockets of the owners, and the fact that a Master is making dollars for his owners is one basis upon which ship owners will naturally judge the efficiency of their Masters.
If this bill as it stands allows that kind of practice to become widespread, it seems to me in some respects we are defeating the basic purpose of the bill which is, as it says, to improve upon the existing provision of pilotage service in a more realistic way, with more local autonomy of judgment as to how detailed management should be carried out in respect of those areas where it is to be applied.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to the hon. member who moved an amendment to clause 15 and to his remarks on the need to provide for the greatest shipping safety within our territorial waters. I do not believe the requirements in this amendment would really improve the safety standards already established in the legislation for the simple reason that, within our shipping zones, there must be a pilot or a holder of a pilotage certificate.
Under an amendment to paragraph (a), subclause (2) of clause 15 of the act, it has been established that accord-
Pilotage Act
ing to the legislation requirements, the holder of a pilotage certificate must, in the opinion of the local authority, have a degree of skill equivalent or at least equal to that of a licence holder. That is why I cannot understand very well why the issuing of pilotage certificates must be limited to Canadian ships only.
While attempting to grant special protection to a certain class we are perhaps depriving a good number of Canadian pilotage certificate holders from becoming crew members of a foreign ship if they so desire.
I am speaking at this stage of the study on this important bill, which was fully discussed in committee, first to express my personal appreciation for the discretion that was granted all members and for the real exercise of democracy that prevailed during consideration of this bill.
I would like to commend the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) who, while piloting this most complicated bill, has allowed hon. members the greatest freedom. The understanding of all the civil servants who participated in the study of this bill should also be recognized.
This is important since, when the bill was studied by the committee substantial amendments were proposed and almost all of them were given unanimous approval. I also commend the hon. member for LaSalle (Mr. Les-sard), chairman of the Transport and Communications committee, who handled with much tact our proceedings on this important question.
Mr. Speaker, during several meetings which were perhaps exhausting but also most important, we were able to discuss in depth an extremely technical bill which is most important for Canadian shipping and which lays down major principles which I want to mention. Among these basic principles I would simply recall at this stage that for nine years we had been waiting for the report of the Royal Commission on Pilotage.
In its report the Commission came to the conclusion that pilotage authority just had to be decentralized. It is proposed in the bill to establish four local authorities which will be in a better position respectively to judge the problems posed by pilotage in Canadian waters.
Decentralization was requested by all interested parties and the bill includes such a proposal. I believe that unless we have absolutely no confidence in the local administration that will so be constituted, we reject the basic principle of this bill, aimed first of all at decentralization. If we do not trust the local administration, we indeed reject the basis of that bill, the essential principle on which the officials relied while drafting that legislation.
Besides decentralization, there is another essential principle that was put forward in the Bernier commission report-that exemptions from compulsory pilotage should be based in future not only on the tonnage or the seaworthiness of the ship but also on the qualifications of the person at the helm. This provides an additional and

June 18, 1971
Pilotage Act
indispensable security factor, because it is well known that traffic is growing heavier within Canadian territorial waters and one quickly must conclude that whatever the size of a ship, small, medium or large, its presence within our waters and in vital pilotage zones may spell great danger.
While studying this legislation in committee, we suggested some amendments. Notwithstanding all the amendments that were made, it is a fact that perhaps some of the people concerned still entertain apprehensions or misgivings about that bill.
In my view, the bill, in its present form, including some corrections to which I would like to draw the minister's attention, is of great importance and represents considerable progress, unless one would want to consider future authorities as incompetent. The bill is an answer to a long-standing need and it attempts to ensure, within Canadian waters, real control of the safety of pilotage.
The previous speaker praised our Canadian pilots. I wish to say that I agree with him wholeheartedly and to add that it is not merely a question of ensuring employment security for an important group of workers-I would say of professionals in the field of shipping-but rather of really understanding to what extent the role which these people have played in the past and will have to play in the future, is pressing and important since we passed Bill C-2 on pollution.
I recently read in a Quebec newspaper an article on the consequences of a ship running aground or of a maritime disaster which could happen at the level of Portneuf, or elsewhere in the St. Lawrence river, up to the Escoumains or Kimouski, because it must be understood to what extent, through tidal movements, a disaster in the river would bring about irreparable and widespread damage.
In the consideration of this legislation we insisted more on the necessity, not to keep pilots but to insure aboard ships sailing in our waters the presence of men whose competence will be controlled by local authorities or by the department, emphasizing the increasing importance of this matter. Some people might feel that clause 14 will enable local authorities to establish new compulsory pilotage areas. However, I fail to see how compulsory pilotage areas could be established in our Canadian waters, where traffic density is very great. In fact, experience has shown that only experts have the qualifications required to conduct ships in these areas.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation provides for establishment of local authorities for the purpose of decentralizing pilotage. To this end, we must choose one of two courses. We can have everything included in the act. Then, it would seem that we do not trust the authority to be set up. On the other hand, we may accept the principle of decentralisation and put our faith in the authority to be set up, with the understanding that the local authority will be closer to the actual problems of navigation and will obviously be more competent to pass judgment on the qualifications of those that are to hold pilotage certificates.
So, as proposed in the bill, I chose to trust the local authority and believe in the regulations that will be set up and published for 30 days in the Canada Gazette under clause 14.
As far as compulsory navigation zones and regulations concerning the qualifications of pilotage certificate holders are concerned, these regulations should be given a 30-day public notice and be subject to investigation.
Within such a framework, I can hardly imagine how the local authorities of the Montreal area, for instance, could intervene while the shipping traffic continues to increase and say or direct that there will be no compulsory pilotage, from Quebec City to Escoumains and that it will not be necessary that a certificate holder be on board one or another of the ships which will negociate the distance.
Under section 14(1)a), it will be possible to awake the public interest and show that it is out of the question to make shipping completely free within our waters.
It is a known fact, Mr. Speaker, that all countries require that a pilot steer the ships travelling in their territorial waters. The reaction to the Darling report is also known. That report, which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) tabled in the House on May 21 last, has been concurred in by almost all ship owners because it made the specific recommendation that Canadian ships be responsible for coastal navigation in territorial waters.
If we are so convinced that it is essential to promote coastal shipping by Canadian vessels, I can easily understand why members of the Committee on Transport and Communications urged that pilotage certificate holders be Canadian citizens or immigrants having filed their citizenship application. The requirement was approved and when I refer to the favourable reaction to the publication of the Darling report recommending that only Canadian ships move goods between ports, I wish to make it clear that it was important to guarantee that Canadians pilot ships in important inland waters called compulsory pilotage areas.
On the whole, that legislation can give rise to some concern. Literally, that legislation could suggest that the local authority, the minister or the cabinet could enact regulations altering its meaning. As a result, we would be introducing a bill to delude the public and I cannot accept such argument. I trust-and I say so in all fairness-the Minister of Transport and his advisers, but Parliament would always be in a position to enact other regulations. However, for the moment I am convinced that the Minister of Transport is quite determined to carry out to the letter the general instructions which will have been recommended to cabinet and included in regulations made by local authorities created once the bill has been approved.
There, actually, is my idea of this law. And if the authorities are not trusted, one may, obviously, through reluctance or by playing with terms, interpret certain clauses as meaning that indeed the cabinet has the power to establish a parallel pilotage system and to get rid of the present system.

June 18, 1971

For my part, I trust the authorities; it they let me down, I can always make representations, as a member of Parliament, to the powers that be, but I feel I shall not have to do so. Not only will I not have to do so, but I am sure that the cabinet that proposed so important a measure is still the one that can best administer it.
I suspect that when the Authority has been set up, some might begin to worry.
As for me, and I say it again, quite frankly, I feel I was one of those who, in committee, presented the views shared by the association of the St. Lawrence pilots.
On the whole, however, this legislation is clear and relevant, and, unless we have no confidence in the future, or see problems where there are none, it is premature to suggest that this legislation does not represent a considerable step forward in the regulation of pilotage in Canada, and this, in the best interest of pilots, whom I shall always try to protect, because they really ensure the security of shipping. Since they are experts, I do not see how, in a system where traffic is constantly increasing, as it is in our compulsory areas, we might eventually reduce their number.
While we are talking about pollution, to allow larger and bigger ships to sail in our waters without direction and control by Canadian experts, by pilots who have been delivered licences or certificates by the Department of Transport, would give the impression that the cabinet, the government, in short, that Parliament has completely lost its mind, and that Members of Parliament do not understand the major interests of the people.
On the whole, I am not only satisfied with the bill, but also with the help provided by the Parliamentary Secretary to the minister, my colleague from Quebec East (Mr. Duquet), as well as the help of all hon. members and the co-operation of the minister who has allowed the true play of democracy. We moved helpful and constructive amendments which, I think, should dispel the fears of those who are primarily interested.

Perhaps the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) will wish to say something briefly on third reading; otherwise, this will be our total contribution on this measure.
Our remarks will be brief, in inverse proportion to the importance of the measure. We agree that it is an important measure. However, such was the success of discussions in the committee that one can say the different
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
issues were well and truly thrashed out. Ample leeway was given. I cannot remember any bill with respect to which so much leeway was given in committee. What we have before us is a fair consensus of what people consider to be important in the bill.
May I first say to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that, although I greatly respect the earnestness of his submission, I cannot unfortunately support it and my colleagues cannot support it. Nevertheless, since he was good enough to say that he was really trying an idea on for size, I do not think he will regret the decision we have made. As a maritime member, I have to think of the effects of legislation on ships of British registry engaged in our coastal trade. On balance, although he has done us a great service by presenting his idea and giving us an opportunity to speak about it, I must reject his contention.
The hon. member, and the hon. member who succeeded him in this debate, outlined the concept of the pilotage certificate. He referred to people who, in limited cases or in limited regions, will be entitled to exercise the rights of pilots, although those people will actually be officers of the ship which they are piloting. That was the main issue before the committee. It was asked, to what extent should this right be given. The responsibility that would rest on the person who is given a pilotage certificate is, in a sense, a responsibility towards Canada. For example, he could come from outside Canada. We made important amendments in this regard and I think, by and large, performed a fair service in not killing the original concept of the bill but putting it within reasonable limits. What really bothered me was that there would be people who could exercise pilots' rights without having a sense of responsibility towards Canada. I think that the curbs put on that class of person were pretty reasonable curbs.
I think the legislation should now have a chance to prove itself, and so I make this suggestion to the minister and to the parliamentary secretary. I think it might even meet the point of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I suggest that a reasonable report regarding the operations of this bill be drawn up-a special study, as it were- that could be presented to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications when the estimates are considered one year from now. I do not think that is asking too much. I think if officials know that they will be expected to come forward with a detailed report upon which they will be questioned, the point raised by my friend for Comox-Alberni will probably be met. That, of course, would certainly meet any hesitation that I might have about the bill and at the same time it would give this important act an opportunity to prove itself in operation. That is the only suggestion I want to make. I put it forward as a respectful request, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the House that I am also a member of the Transport and Communications Committee and, when the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme) gives to understand that everything went on smoothly and in a
June 18, 1971

democratic way during the study of this famous bill, one has to take it with a grain of salt.
The story of democracy is rather the story of pressure because it is known that the association of pilots had delegated one of its members to the committee and requested an hon. member to present many amendments. But after a few days of negociation, the member who had introduced the main amendment was forced to withdraw it under pressure from the authorities because it can-tradicted senior officials in the Canadian government.
Being very much aware of the excellent work done by the Royal Commission on Pilotage, I am disappointed that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) did not see fit to accept all the recommendations of the Commission, especially that which to me is the most important, pilotage on the St. Lawrence River.
Clause 14(1) states that the authority can determine areas of compulsory pilotage.
I believe that such power is to be feared, though I realize that it could be checked through some rule or commission. I am convinced that there are areas of the St. Lawrence where no pilotage authority should be allowed to overrule compulsory pilotage provisions.
The most important places insofar as Canadian shipping is concerned are the rivers and waterways most sensitive with respect to the Canadian economy as a whole. Nobody could suggest that the St. Lawrence River is not one of them.
Besides, I could never support a decision to deprive of their jobs Canadian pilots and their families. For those reasons, I take strong exception to the clauses of this bill which could lead to the removal of the regulation requiring the presence of a Canadian pilot on-board ships in the St. Lawrence River.
In that connection, I would like to quote parts of Part I of the report of the Royal Commission on Pilotage. On page 233, under the title "Freedom of Pilotage Service", one can read the following:
Local knowledge and experience in local navigation are the ultimate and most essential requirements for safe navigation in confined waters. Since the raison d'etre of organized pilotage is to provide shipping with the services of qualified navigators who are experts in navigating local confined waters, an efficient and adequate pilotage service is the ultimate means of enhancing safety of navigation.
As a rule, compulsory pilotage should be imposed: (a) on Masters who do not possess the necessary degree of local knowledge to navigate their ship or navigation unit safely; (b) in ship channels where a maritime disaster would seriously affect the economy of the country and the interest of the public.
Because pilotage is the most effective way of achieving safety of navigation, it should come under the jurisdiction of the authorities responsible for the safety of navigation, wherever such safety is of vital importance to the country. Conversely, the involvement of these authorities is not as necessary where the safety of navigation is not an essential national concern.
Here is now the most important part of the text:
For instance, nowhere is the safety of ship channels more vital to Canadian interests than on the St. Lawrence River.
Pilotage Act
Considering the great importance of pilotage on the St. Lawrence River, I think the provisions on compulsory pilotage should be included in the legislation and that the rather broad powers referred to on page 233 of Part I of the report be given to authorities. Furthermore, the Commission suggests that the future legislation on pilotage deal mainly with safety of navigation.
Surely navigation is nowhere more important than on the St. Lawrence River.
In fact, the St. Lawrence River is treacherous, and this has been recognized by the Commission. I live in Don-nacona and I can see the Quebec City bridge from my house. This waterway is 30 miles long and three miles wide, yet when a ship runs aground everyone notices. As long as the whales stay in the water, nobody cares. But as soon as a whale emerges, the people of the village come rushing to see what is the commotion.
Along the St. Lawrence River, especially in the Port-neuf region, you do not have to go on the beach. From my window, I once saw a ship around at Saint-Nicolas; at Saint-Augustin, on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, I could see another ship, outside the channel, on the reef. Recently, the same thing happened at Cap-Sante; a ship went out of the channel and it looked for a moment as if it migh run aground on the coast. Then the strollers collected along the shore, looked on and worried.
Not too long ago, the same thing happened in Leclerc-ville. A few years back, there was a shipwreck in the Petite Riviere Saint-Frangois in which Chinese sailors perished. And, closer to Quebec City, in the channel at the bottom of the river near the lie d'Orleans, another wreck still remains a danger.
There is already too much freedom under the regulations. Pilotage duties are being charged to ships entering the river, but there is nothing to force them to retain the services of a pilot. So, you get a pretty fair idea of what happens to those regulations that are often applied according to the captain's or the shipping companies' sense of responsibility. The St. Lawrence is dangerous. A maritime disaster could greatly affect the Canadian economy and the public interest. The Channel is indeed of vital significance to the country.
So, on the national level, the St. Lawrence channel should be a seaway where compulsory pilotage is guaranteed. I would not like to see such a decision left to one administration with only the possibility to appeal to the minister. I would rather like to see compulsory pilotage on the St. Lawrence included in bill C-246 and at a later stage, I will move an amendment to this effect.
Yet, I would like to emphasize the situation of pilots; the report admits that pilotage on the St. Lawrence is of extreme importance. To me, the best way to ensure good pilotage on the river is to require Canadian pilots to be on duty on all ships sailing on the river. To my mind, no other means is adequate to comply with navigation security standards.
At the same time, it must be kept in mind that pilotage is a special profession which requires a long and difficult training, which means that pilots, although experts in this field, could not easily adjust to other types of employment. Indeed, there are not many fields in which

they could put their training to use. So, in the interest of security, everything should be done to prevent these pilots from being laid off. I would not want to see this happen under a by-law; it would be completely unfair.
If the act provides for compulsory pilotage along the Pacific coast, I would like to hear the minister say, when he rises, in the name of what freedom an authority would be allowed to make decisions in the Quebec area which, after all, is the most dangerous and should actually have been the one to cause no concern. All the necessary clauses should have been included in this bill to ensure first of all, security for the Canadian public, and especially employment security for this group of pilots who have been efficient and very active until now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the member opposite who was defending his opposition to this amendment. I was surprised at his view of the amendment. I agree that things are tough in Canada and that we need to create jobs. There is no question about that. However, this bill is much too important to consider creating opportunities for people who have the potential of getting a mate's licence for Canadian waters to be employed by a foreign power.
While I did not have the opportunity of listening to the deliberations of the committee, in past years I have been very interested in the job that has been done by the Department of Transport. The job has not always been entirely satisfactory to the Department of Transport but we have developed, particularly in our inland waters, a remarkable crew of men. They have handled an immense amount of shipping from all parts of the world despite language problems, different customs and differences in the types of charts and measurements that we use. These people have been able to come into Canadian waters and use the seaway facilties to their advantage and ours. This has been possible because of the calibre of people registered as pilots under the Canada Shipping Act.
In moving this amendment, my colleague had in mind the point made by the previous speaker, namely that this would be an opportune time for creating jobs for Canadians. Anyone who had obtained either a pilot's or an apprentice pilot's licence for any waters under Canada's authority would have been able to work as first or second mate and bring a ship in to Canadian waters without the necessity of hiring a Canadian pilot. While this would create some jobs, it would not be satisfactory to the pilots who have established this reputation. It would not be acceptable to the Canadian authorities or public because Canadian pilots have developed a great deal of independence. They have had their ups and downs.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mar. Barnett) referred to one case where there is a difference of opinion as to whether the master should be able to do what he wants. The pilot said, no. A second pilot was asked for his assistance and was pushed into taking the vessel out under conditions less than favourable. The fact that the ship went to the bottom interests only the insurance
company, I suppose. But there is an important lesson to be learned from this. Those who are working continuously in short portions of our waterways are in a position from day to day to drop into the pilotage centres and discuss with other pilots changing conditions which may be developing, the congestion anticipated from the presence of other sripping, changes which have been made in the placement of navigational aids, and so on.
If we allow those holding pilotage certificates to ship on vessels of foreign register and act in any capacity other than that of captain, they will be placed in a position where their wishes can be overridden at any time. Moreover, as the hon. member who spoke from the government benches noted, a great possibility for developing Canadian job opportunities on foreign ships will be eliminated.
It has been interesting to discuss pilotage matters with those directly affected. One of the difficulties has been that the Department of Transport has failed to keep abreast of changing conditions and changing needs; it has not responded to these changes nearly as fast as the shipping companies or the pilotage authorities. The pilots and the representatives of the shipping companies have on a number of occasions insisted on the updating of navigational aids which the department argued that it was not in a position to provide because of monetary considerations. A few years ago serious difficulties arose on the St. Lawrence on a number of occasions because of the department's inability to purchase up-to-date radio equipment for the use of our pilots. The equipment they were using was largely ineffective by comparison with that which could be purchased from other countries. It was only after a parliamentary committee had given great study to this question that the department could be prodded into working in conjunction with the National Research Council to develop suitable equipment.
The dialogue which has been going on between the Pilots Association and the government in conjunction with the shipping companies has produced for Canada a fairly responsible body which has done more for Canadian shipping than was anticipated. I express the hope in connection with pilotage that either we make it mandatory within certain areas to carry a pilot, or else develop a higher degree of skill in certain very concise areas. I am thinking particularly of the passage through the Seaway locks where a high degree of skill is necessary. If we put a pilot aboard in the basin at Montreal and go through the St. Lambert locks, a passage which calls for a high degree of skill, I suggest that the pilot so employed should not be used in areas where their particular skill would be largely wasted. Pilots who lack that particular expertise could well be used in such areas. This observation, of course, applies to other areas.
One of the principal areas with which I am concerned, because it is of great importance to this country over the next few years, is the area to be included in the schedule under the Great Lakes Pilotage Authority. As most people are aware, Canada is divided into four pilotage regions-Atlantic, Pacific, Laurentian and Great Lakes.

June 18, 1971

While the Great Lakes system is probably the largest inland water system in the world, that particular authority is also responsible for shipping in another very large area, the Hudson Bay and James Bay area. The reason I make the point about the advantage of specialization, particularly in the Seaway, is that I would be strongly opposed to the authority sending out pilots to operate in the Hudson Bay-James Bay area. I think it would be unfair to the pilots concerned and detrimental to the operation of the pilotage authority. We have not as yet developed any expertise in the field of Arctic shipping. It is true there are some experts, probably three or four of top calibre. But from the information available to me these are not the people who are running our icebreakers; they are not the people who are employed by the Department of Transport at the present time.
However, there are a number of people who are experts in this field and have spent a great deal of time in northern and Arctic ice. I am pleased that the government is interesting itself in this field. I was also pleased to note that one of the places that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) visited in Russia, when he was paying some attention to problems there similar to those in Canada, was Murmansk. At this northern Arctic port they had developed a degree of expertise that had enabled them for a number of years not only to operate the port, which is ice-free and much above the normal shipping lanes, but to navigate ships in what is an iceberg area, which we are not able to do. I am sure that the Prime Minister and his officials will be giving some attention to this problem.
I suggest that the authority now being given to the Great Lakes Pilotage Authority should not extend to Hudson Bay. This is a new authority that should be centred upon the Churchill area. The Hudson Bay route is not operated by Canada today; it is really operated from London by Lloyds and other insurance companies. These are the companies which determine when the season starts and when it ends. They exercise authority similar to that which insurance companies used to exercise in the Great Lakes area.
We have extended considerably both the spring and fall shipping seasons on the Great Lakes system, having developed the expertise to close the seaway on a daily or weekly basis. Ships in the seaway are given 24 or 48 hours' notice of closure and this is found to be sufficient. The situation is not the same in the Hudson Bay area, a shipping lane that has many advantages both for western Canada and northern Europe. This is an area of great development potential as well as great need. The committee would have been well advised to seize itself of the question of the Hudson Bay shipping authority and to recommend an authority in that area to meet some of the problems of which most members of the House are aware.
I hope hon. members will give consideration to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-24171-161
Pilotage Act
Alberni (Mr. Barnett). In addition, I hope that one of
these days the House will show interest not only in the establishment of a pilotage authority for Hudson Bay but also in other coastal areas of Canada. It strikes me as very odd that a representative of the government should suggest that we train people in Canada for their mate's certificate; that they apply for a pilotage certificate simply so they can get a job on a Liberian freighter. This seems to me a rather odd situation.
It also seems odd that we are making large contributions free of interest to one of the maritime shipbuilding industries to enable them to build ships for France. Why do we not build these ships for ourselves without interest and operate them under Canadian registry? On top of that, a representative of the government is suggesting that we train people to navigate ships so that the owners do not have to pay pilotage fees when passing through Canadian waters.
It strikes me that one point that has been overlooked is that we have one of the longest coastlines in the world. We do not have sufficient expertise in regard to fishing zones, fishing rights, protection of ships in inland waters and passages; indeed, it is only within the last five or six years that we have concerned ourselves with this problem. We are now suggesting we train crews to serve on the ships of other countries. We are building ships to sail under other registries. Although we are providing the wherewithal to do this, we still have made no decision to build our own merchant navy. Some might say that we are not in a position to build one. If that is the case, I would remind them that prior to the last war Canada had a very small merchant navy. After the war we ranked third or fourth in the commercial shipping interests of the world. Those ships were under Canadian registry and operated by Canadian crews. Not only did these crews handle Canadian ships but also the shipping of other countries. Therefore, I suggest it is possible to develop an interest in Canadian shipping.
However, I suggest we will not develop an interest in Canadian shipping by following the course the government seems bent upon, of supplying competent assistance to foreign ships navigating in Canadian waters. Rather, we should place greater reliance on Canadians being employed on ships which are pledged to serve Canadian interests.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now under consideration is quite important and I would like to insist on its consequences especially concerning the pilots on the St. Lawrence.
Mr. Speaker, my constituency includes several municipalities situated on the shores of the St. Lawrence and consequently pilots are taxpayers of those municipalities. I am therefore in a position to know about their problems and to state my views during consideration of that bill providing for the establishment of new authorities.

June 18, 1971
Pilotage Act
A little earlier I wanted to put a very simple question to the hon. member tor Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme). I know he has been deeply involved and has done an excellent job in taking up the cudgels on behalf of the St. Lawrence pilots, but I must admit that he did not get his way along the line, which I regret.
The hon. member for Montmorency expressed his very great confidence in the hon. minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) as well as in all the officials of the department. I am only too willing to see this confidence become positive so that he may do justice to all those affected by the bill.
Mr. Speaker, parliamentary, political experience has shown us that it can be dangerous to have confidence in government administration. That is why it is always better that in such legislation things are spelled out, in order that they be clear and unequivocal.
I am not imputing motives to anyone, but good intentions must be protected.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this bill shows a will to organize properly the various pilotage authorities in Canadian waters, a will to protect against pollution, a will to protect the sovereignty of Canadian territories. But I wonder to what extent we safeguard the principle of Canadian sovereignty in Canadian territorial waters when we leave clauses in the bill indicating that in some cases, pilots and foreigners might be allowed to navigate our waters freely, without the support of our competent pilots who know their trade, and on the tip of their fingers-to use the popular expression-the nooks and corners of the St. Lawrence river, and who consequently can lead in all safety the ships that navigate it.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is a basic principle that is not even questionable, that in our own waters, and especially in the St. Lawrence-which is, as everyone knows, the heart of Quebec and the greatest waterway in Canada-we should be assured that any ship which passes through it are protected by Canadian pilots.
Mr. Speaker, I readily believe in the good intentions that the hon. member for Montmorency ascribes to the minister, but I am not sure about them. This is why I would have preferred that the amendments suggested by the Federation of St. Lawrence River Pilots were more favourably considered and defended-I would not say more energetically, since I am sure that the hon. member for Montmorency acted in good faith and did his best- which would have resulted in the support of his colleagues in committee and caused all the amendments to be adopted. In my opinion, they were basic and necessary.
For instance, I should like to make only a few points to better illustrate my own approach. In clause 14(c)-
(c) prescribing the circumstances under which compulsory pilotage may be waived;
the pilots had suggested that we add the following:
*-for Canadian ships of less than 350 registered tons.
Mr. Speaker, why have these words not been added? Which influence was exerted to convince the members of the standing committee on Transport and Communications to refuse such amendments, while they guaranteed not only protection for the members of the Federation of St. Lawrence River Pilots, but, besides-since an essential principle was at stake, sovereignty, the protection of the ships and of the associations as well-respect for a profession which in the past has proved its efficiency and absolute necessity beyond any doubt?
Mr. Speaker, I wish here to deplore the situation and this is why I make my point. I wanted to put a question to the hon. member for Montmorency were it not for an interference from the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger)-who never takes the floor and who now seems quite mad at the members of the Ralliement creditiste. I simply wanted to ask him if the Association of the St. Lawrence river pilots agreed with his statements. It is the urgent question I wanted to ask him since now in Canada, we are facing problems of all kinds and, among others, a major constitutional problem. Even though the various federal-provincial conferences, as everybody knows, do not solve anything, it has turned out to be a major problem.
In the province of Quebec, when an association almost exclusively from Quebec is thus denied a greater protection, some question must be asked, but this does not solve the major problems now facing Canada in this connection.
I suggest that the Minister of Transport should consider giving special attention to the recommendations made by this association, and I still hope that my colleagues on the government side will look fully into the matter-most especially the Quebec members-so as to safeguard, in Quebec, the scope, the strength and the purpose of such an important association in such an important field as navigation, namely the Association of the St. Laurence river pilots.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks with this wish: I would like that the confidence referred to by the member for Montmorency could turn into concrete regulations the very legislation now under study in this House.

Mr. Speaker, before this bill passes I wish to indicate that I believe this is a good measure which carries out the recommendations of the pilotage commission. I have just looked at the recommendations and I believe there were 39. At quick glance, it would appear that most of them have been fulfilled in some way. Changes were made in the committee. I think that was done in a straightforward manner. The officials of the Department of Transport came forward, gave evidence and accepted many of the proposals which were made. I hope this has made it a better bill. Most of the problems centred around the St. Lawrence. Some of us were loathe to become too closely involved in this, but many members from that area had suggestions. We hope the suggestions which are now coming forward will mean new modern navigation safety, that there will be a protection for the honourable profession of pilots and that Canada itself will be in a better position in respect of world shipping.
The pilotage commission makes reference to the fact that there should be an up-to-date review from time to time in respect of the problems relative to pilotage, and I hope this recommendation is carried forward. I hope a close check is made concerning modem changes which might be implemented. The minister has made changes in his department. I am always suspicious that many of these changes which are said to involve decentralization still involve the retention of authority pretty close to the centre of the department. However, regardless of whether or not this is true, this legislation is a move which I think, after a long review of this subject, may have some good results for those of us who are concerned about where we are going in respect of shipping these days. The minister was not too involved in this legislation. He gave his officials carte blanche and most of us felt they did a good job. But I hope he considers this small piece of legislation only a challenge for the future.
I know the minister has a large department. There are many problems. Previous ministers, who shall be nameless now, left many problems in abeyance while dashing around the country worrying about things in no way connected with transport. The minister appears to have some interest in this field, and he would appear to be energetic. I hope he does not feel that the problems
Pilotage Act
concerning shipping are over now. I hope he will take the Darling Keport home with him to Newfoundland on his holidays so that when he comes back in the fall he will have a brand new marine policy. We will be able to write his name into shipping history if he does.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether the minister intends to reply at the third reading stage to the presentation of my hon. friend. If he does, I should like to repeat for him the suggestion I made at the committee stage. While it is true that this legislation provides for the appointment of any authority, there is this whole new field of Hudson Bay and the high Arctic which I believe should be considered as a separate problem. It would seem to me we have not paid much attention to this area. We are just at the beginning of shipping in that area. Because of this, we should be training people specifically for employment in that area. I believe the Canadian people are so concerned with pollution of all kinds that they will be very sceptical about the idea of allowing any foreign ships into that area without a pilot. People who have spent 30 or 40 years in the high Arctic, in the marine field, indicate there is an immense amount to be learned by anyone who would be involved in the navigation of ships in that area, taking into consideration the limitations in respect of navigational aids for the area.
This is a new field in which we will have to have new types of equipment for the detection of icebergs, shoals and so on. During the committee hearings we heard an interesting history of what has been taking place over the last five or six years. I should like to congratulate the committee for the work it has done in this respect. I should also like to congratulate the department for having arrived at this decision, after what I consider to be one hell of a slow start on the part of many departmental officials. So, we have arrived at this stage. I think Canada will have to provide leadership in a totally new field, the Arctic. I would suggest that if we go into this field in the next year we should separate the high Arctic and Hudson Bay because in my opinion within the next few years consideration will be given to a great extension, probably a doubling, of the length of the shipping season into Hudson Bay. I should like to see a Hudson Bay authority established separately so that we could take full advantage of any pressure the government may be able to apply to make it possible for shipments to move to northern Europe from the midwest without the necessity of going through the present process.
