speechtext:
I assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the minister that it is not my intention to speak at length on third reading of this bill. It is my hope that the bill will pass this afternoon, particularly since the end of the session is fast approaching and there is still much agricultural legislation to be passed. Therefore, I think it would be wise for the House to allow Bill C-239, dealing with cash advances, to be passed.
This legislation was originally introduced back in 1957. It is remarkable how successful it has been among the Prairie producers. When the bill was submitted to the House the minister said that 51,285 individual advances had been made to producers. There were around 185,000 producers in the three Prairie provinces in what is called the Wheat Board region.
This gives hon. members some idea of the service this legislation has provided to the farmers. A little over 25 per cent of the farmers had availed themselves of the cash advances program at the time the legislation was presented, and the number was twice as high sometimes during the winter months. Losses have been minimal. This proves beyond doubt that the legislation has merit. When one thinks back to the stormy period of its birth, one realizes that the minister of the day and those who brought this legislation forward-the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was then Prime Minister-were responsible for instigating it and ensuring its passage. A number of interesting changes have been made to the legislation and after this bill passes and applications are made under it in the new crop year I am certain that members of the House from the Prairie
regions, as well as farmers throughout the Wheat Board region, will watch the changes to see whether they in fact help the agricultural industry.
The most interesting change made in committee dealt with the repayment of loans and interest rates. Until the bill is passed cash advances are interest free, but when it is passed they will continue to be interest free only if they are repaid in grain and if farmers are not in default in their payments. If they are in default, the minister can charge interest on the loan from the time it was taken out until it is repaid.
This has been an interesting bill to study in light of the committee's work. The bill was debated at length in the House on second reading and the minister complained about the lengthy debate. But because we on this side of the House and other hon. members spoke on the provisions of the bill, the minister himself moved an amendment in committee. This points out the merit of thorough discussion of a bill before it is sent to committee, because undoubtedly when the minister recommends an amendment to the committee it has a much greater chance of being accepted than if an ordinary backbencher moves one as a member of the committee.
Although I do not want to mention it, it is regrettable that when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) recommended an amendment to another piece of legislation before the agricultural committee, the members of the committee deliberately rejected it. It is regrettable that such things happen and that when the Prime Minister appoints a person to a portfolio he is not of high enough calibre to command the support of the committee handling the minister's legislation; yet this has taken place.
I would like to explain this amendment because I think it is important. If a cash advance is taken, is repaid wholly in grain and repayment is not in default, no interest is charged on the cash advance. If a cash advance is taken and paid mostly in grain, but in order to finalize the payment of the cash advance the farmer repays some of it in cash, the minister recommended to the committee that if the portion that is paid in cash is not higher than $500 no interest would be required on the cash advance. If it is greater than $500, the recipient would be charged interest from the time the loan was taken out until it was fully repaid.
The fact that the minister was prepared to recommend to the committee the $500 clause and the committee was prepared to accept it, is to the credit of the minister and the committee because in many cases when a farmer takes out a cash advance he does so on the basis of his estimate of the amount of grain in his granaries and in some cases he is too optimistic. Sometimes when a farmer harvests the grain and puts it in the granaries he thinks he has a lot of grain, but when he takes it to the elevator and has it weighed he finds there is not as much as he thought. One must take into account the amount lost through dockage and shrinkage.
This $500 cash payment, without affecting the interest rate on the cash advance allows for some computable error in the amount of grain the farmer may have in the

June 18, 1971

granary. But another factor that comes into play is that many grain farmers who are also in the livestock business-and in the livestock business one never knows how much feed will be required for the winter months-have a tendency to keep a portion of their grain as a reserve feed back for the winter months. As a result, they have less grain to sell. This could bring about variants which would require the farmer to pay the balance in cash. Therefore, to my way of thinking this is a great improvement in the bill.
There is another amendment which the committee accepted on the recommendation of the minister. I want to deal with it because it is a very important and significant change from the original legislation. The original legislation in 1957 set out the exact amount that a person could receive in the way of a cash advance, through the elevator company, from the Canadian Wheat Board for grain in storage on the farm. In the original instance a person could collect 50 cents per bushel of wheat, and when he sold the grain the elevator company was supposed to take back half its value to pay the cash advance. That concept has been changed in this legislation. We see here an undetermined cash advance and an undetermined rate of repayment.
In committee the minister proposed an amendment to this clause, which was accepted. The minister should be commended for the fact that the agricultural committee supports him and has confidence in his recommendations. He recommended that the prescribed rate be determined before the commencement of the crop year. This means that in the spring the farmer will know how much cash advance he will receive on grain in storage on his farm. The amount will change from year to year, but he will be given notice. This is an improvement and needed to be written into the bill. Farming today is geared to meet market demand and the farmer needs to know how much money will be available for the various types of grain. If there should happen to be a slow market for a particular commodity, the farmer can then adjust his production.
There is one other matter I should like to deal with, Mr. Speaker. At the moment there are three major pieces of agricultural legislation before the House, Bills C-238, C-239 and C-244. When the House adjourned last June 26 we found ourselves in the same position of having to push agricultural legislation through quickly. We are down to the wire again; as I understand the rules of the House, Monday will be the last full day available for government legislation. These three pieces of legislation appear to be at the low end of the totem pole so far as the priorities of this government are concerned. I remember making the same remarks a year ago with regard to agricultural legislation.
We cannot be asked to turn a blind eye to so many pieces of agricultural legislation. Sooner or later we must examine them. They are of great concern to the farmer and many people whose livelihood is affected. There are
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act in my office at present 2,500 letters on the subject of Bill C-244 and the chairman of the agricultural committee stated this morning that there is a demand for six to eight groups who wish to appear before the committee on Bill C-238. So there is a great anxiety about some of this legislation. It is a pity that we have come down to the wire again with agricultural legislation apparently having the lowest priority of this government.
We dealt with Bill C-244 in committee rather quickly this morning. On October 29, 1970, the minister announced the proposals that led to the drafting of Bill C-244 and we did not hear anything more about it until last March 15. About a month ago the bill was presented to the House and it went back to committee three weeks ago. We have to hear witnesses on it and pass 37 clauses-

I am not going to argue whether it was four weeks ago or five weeks ago, but where was the bill from October 29? When I asked the minister that question this morning in committee, he replied that they had been out trying to sell it across the country, trying to convince the people that it was good legislation.
The letters we are receiving show what the farmers think of it. I said I had 2,500 letters. I have not asked my secretary whether she made an exact count today, but every member of the agricultural committee has received from 2,000 to 5,000 letters, depending on the anxiety in his constituency. It could have been dealt with and then they could have gone out and sold it to the farmers, to agri-business, and so on. Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I end my remarks with the hope that next June will not find us again trying to cram through agricultural legislation at the last minute. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RATE PER BUSHEL, EMERGENCY PAYMENTS, EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO RYE, FLAXSEED AND RAPESEED
speechtext:
In rising to speak on Bill C-239, Mr. Speaker, I would remind hon. members and the farmers that this is only one of many pieces of legislation on our plate that could be effective in markedly changing the agricultural situation. I have no great quarrel with the provisions of Bill C-239. I support the principle of the bill; it is tidying up and bringing up to date legislation that has proved valuable in the past and will be necessary in the future. This bill is somewhat more restrictive than its predecessor but in general I

June 18, 1971
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
support it as being reasonable and necessary, particularly in regard to the situation of the grain industry in western Canada.
I should like to comment on a few of the problems which this legislation will help solve. It is important to farmers because these are days of opportunity in world food markets and we are hardly getting our share. United States farmers are the pace-setters today; their exports rose to a record $7.2 billion in 1970. That country is looking forward to even greater farm export sales. President Nixon hailed the surging vitality of United States agriculture and pledged to help farmers realize more of its rewards. He set a goal of $10 billion for farm exports from the United States. Since some people think that nearly all United States farm produce benefits from support prices, it is interesting to note that 60 per cent of United States farm income comes from commodities that are not included in price support programs.
United States Secretary of Agriculture C. H. Hardin further emphasized the importance that the United States government places on the value of exports. He boasted that almost one cropland acre out of four in that country is contributing to exports. He pointed out that his country is exporting commodities such as wheat, feed grains and soybeans, areas in which the United States is directly competing with Canada inasmuch as we seek to sell our wheat, barley and rapeseed. He was reported as saying:
Our greatest opportunity for market growth lies in exports. We have the ability to produce with great efficiency, particularly in the major bulkshipped commodities such as wheat, feed grains, and soybeans.
He went on to say that the new agricultural act gives farmers greater flexibility. I ask, what is the situation facing farmers in Canada? In this country problems have arisen in agriculture inasmuch as provinces are worrying about their agricultural position and have brought about the chicken and egg war as well as engaging in other, similar actions. It has become evident that the more populous provinces are worried and are having a hard time keeping out the produce of less populous provinces. This is not good. Ottawa responded with Bill C-176, an inward-looking bill which is not likely to be of any significant help in this area. We shall have to see whether Bill C-176, if passed, will have the effect of bringing about a common market in this country. I was always under the impression that a common market referred to many countries working together and not to the various provinces of one country working together. That was the impression left by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Manitoba, as well as other western provinces, will be affected by this legislation. Mr. Speaker, four or five years can make a great difference in this area.
The Ryerson Press, which is now under foreign control, in 1966 prepared for publication a book to help celebrate the first 100 years of Canada's history. The author wrote an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of Monday, June 14, 1971, which reads in part:
In recent years, thanks partly to massive sales to China, Russia and other countries behind the iron curtain, prairie wheat farmers have become prosperous as never before.
What a difference a few years makes. Ryerson, the oldest continuously operating publishing house in Canada, has fallen into foreign hands. The prairie wheat farmer, beset by government regulation and declining markets, hardly knows which way to turn. He feels trapped in a long, dark tunnel with no sign of light at the end.
Those remarks apply to wheat farmers and other farmers big or small. The article continues:
As one farmer expressed it, "It is getting to the place where I may as well be nothing more than the hired man on my own farm-except that as a hired man I'd be better paid. I have one of the best farms in this community, but I haven't made a cent on my farm operation in the last three years. I'm living on what should be laid aside for depreciation. My property tax bill this year was almost $3,000, $1,900 of it representing the school tax. There is no way in which I can battle forever against such odds.''
The bill before us will go some way in relieving that situation but it will not solve the problem. The article then reads:
The two rays of light in a dark situation are that, with Bill C-176 apparently headed for the discard, traditional cattle markets will stay open-and there is some hope of a greater movement of wheat. But even the latter is small comfort. More than one farmer has wheat still on hand that he harvested four years ago. Increased quotas this year may alleviate his predicament but it will not solve his long-range problem.
It seems to me that farmers in Manitoba and western Canada generally have legitimate gripes and axes to grind. Only three years ago our farmers were told to grow all the wheat they could because there was an unlimited market for it. The farmers are bitter about the Lower Inventory for Tomorrow, or Lift program of last year which cut down wheat acreage but which was less than beneficial financially to farmers. Indeed, we are passing the legislation now before the House in order to help the farmer. He is critical of what he considers lack of aggressive selling policy on the part of the Wheat Board. He distrusts what the Free Press has called the "Ottoman empire of Otto Lang" and feels plagued by government interference and regulations in the entire conduct of the wheat industry. I have spoken of some of the things which affect wheat farmers in Manitoba as well as farmers in other parts of the Prairies.
According to figures relating to the agricultural industry of Manitoba, in 1968 the farmers' cash income was $365 million. In 1969 it had declined to $351 million and in 1970 it was $336 million, a drop of $29 million over a period of three years. We get the same picture from an examination of realized net income. This stood at $114 million in 1968, at $109 million in 1969 and at $94 million in 1970. There we see that over the same period farm income dropped by about $20 million. Farmers whose income has not increased or whose income has decreased are still faced with ever-increasing costs; prices have not stood still. The same sort of thing has happened all over Canada. Taxes and equipment costs continue to rise. As a result there is extreme dissatisfaction in the rural areas of western Canada.
I will support this bill as being a small measure in the right direction but it is in no way a complete answer to our problems. Further legislation, it is hoped, will be

June 18, 1971

introduced to improve it. However, I find the legislation valuable at this time.

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF REGIONAL TREATMENT
PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF REGIONAL TREATMENT
subsubtopic: CENTRES TO DEAL WITH NON-MEDICAL DRUG ABUSE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a system of regional drug treatment centres and co-ordination for a region or province and which would be capable of providing treatment for drug dependency, of co-ordinating the activities of treatment satel-

June 18, 1971
Non-Medical Drug Abuse Treatment Centres
lites or subclinics, and oi working with other social and governmental agencies to provide a non-punitive treatment approach to the drug abuse problem.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it has become a cliche to say that ours is a drug-oriented society: the fact is well known. Every day people rely on some type of drug, whether it be a sleeping pill, a cigarette, a scotch and soda, a teaspoon of cough medicine or a couple of aspirins, in order to function. The number of Canadians using drugs for non-medical purposes has reached an alarming level and there is every indication that it is on the increase.
Consider, if you will, Mr. Speaker, the following statistics beginning with the drug that continues to present the most serious problem-alcohol. Since 1951 alcoholism has increased by almost 60 per cent while per capita consumption of alcohol has increased by approximately 25 per cent. The Le Dain commission records that while in 1951 there were 117,685 convictions for offences involving alcohol, by 1966 this figure had risen to 302,278, an increase of more than 150 per cent. These convictions accounted for a total of between 8.5 per cent and 6.3 per cent of convictions for all crimes in Canada during those years.
What about narcotics? Although the opiate narcotic addict population has declined in proportion to the population as a whole, the number of young narcotic addicts rose from 1 per cent in 1968 to 4 per cent in 1970. Convictions for possession of heroin increased from 310 in 1969 to 383 in 1970, while the number of convictions for trafficking in heroin jumped from 89 in 1969 to 180 in 1970. With regard to so-called restricted drugs such as LSD, MDA and DMT, we again find that usage is up. For instance, on the basis of convictions it can be fairly accurately assumed that LSD use almost trippled in Canada between the years 1968 and 1970.
The story is much the same in the category known as controlled drugs. The increase in the abuse of amphetamines is of major concern today, and cases of barbiturate overdoses are up sharply. In 1967 there were 478 reported barbiturate poisoning cases compared to 197 in 1961. Couple these figures with the 973 minor tranquillizer poisoning cases in 1969, compared to a total of 63 cases in 1961, and the trend is brought sharply into focus.
As for marijuana, presently the most controversial drug, determining the extent of its use is complicated by the fact that some users who believe they have smoked marijuana have, in reality, smoked substances. However, it has been estimated that in 1970, 18.3 per cent of the Canadian population used marijuana compared to 6.7 per cent in 1968. Perhaps even more significant are the figures released earlier this month which indicate that convictions for possession totalled 5,399 last year compared with a low of 11 in 1962. The 1970 figure represents an increase of 3,086 from the previous year. From the foregoing statistics, Mr. Speaker, it becomes apparent that in relative terms at least it is difficult to overstate the gravity of the drug abuse problem in Canada today. It is a serious problem and has been approached as such
by this government which, quite rightly I believe, has refused to be swayed by extremists at either end of the spectrum.
We all await with interest and hope the final report of the Le Dain commission. The sense of urgency present in the recommendations of its interim report was echoed late last January by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) with the announcement of a significant new federal program to combat drug abuse. I am proposing today that the government consider an extension of that very valuable program by setting up a system of regional drug treatment centres to provide a non-punitive treatment approach, present reliable information and co-ordinate the activities of treatment satellites or subclinics. This would be a logical extension of the present program.
As I see them, these regional centres, which would not necessarily have to be administered by the government itself, would be staffed by a multidisciplinary group of medical specialists, social workers and non-professional youth workers. The regional centres would interact with and exercise general supervision over innovative services operated at the municipal level. I foresee such local services having a great deal of participation from community groups and young people themselves.
e (4:10p.m.)
The active involvement of empathetic, sensitive young persons in both the regional and local treatment centres would be extremely desirable if the younger drug users are to be helped. Far too often the younger user is reluctant to seek help from the established hospital system and thus is only given care at a very extreme stage of illness. This reluctance stems partly from his fear of being reported to the police by the hospital authorities and partly from the well known negative attitude of many hospital staff members toward drug users.
Clinics locally operated within a guiding framework laid down by the regional treatment centres would be the solution to this very real and practical problem. This innovative services approach has worked well in Montreal which is fortunate enough to be reasonably well supplied with youth clinics and street agencies. In fact, it has worked so well that the Montreal police now usually take young people suffering bad trips to one of the youth clinics rather than to the emergency department of a hospital.
It would be important to ensure that the regional treatment centres and their local clinics operate on a nonpunitive basis with no suggestion that they are acting as just another branch of a law enforcement network. However, consideration should be given to making it possible for the courts to use the centres as rehabilitation clinics, referring drug offenders to the regional centres rather than imposing fines or jail sentences which serve little useful purpose either for the individual or for society as a whole. The centres would handle each case individually, suggesting to the user the best program for rehabilitation. Only by exposing the person to the facts about drug

June 18, 1971

abuse and showing him the possibility of functioning independently of drugs can we hope for a well adjusted human being. Experience has shown that treating him as a criminal is likely to only reinforce his drug-taking habit.
I have tried in this brief presentation this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, to demonstrate that the drug abuse problem in Canada is increasing dramatically and to show how I believe the existing federal fight against drug abuse should be expanded to meet the growing threat to the mental and physical well-being of our nation. Admittedly, the program I am proposing is an ambitious one. It is as ambitious as the problem is serious. I hope the House will agree with me that the plan should receive favourable consideration.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF REGIONAL TREATMENT
subsubtopic: CENTRES TO DEAL WITH NON-MEDICAL DRUG ABUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my hon. friend from Burnaby-Rich-mond-Delta (Mr. Goode) for having placed this motion on the order paper recommending that the government should consider establishing a system of regional drug treatment centres.
It seems to me my hon. friend is anticipating some of the recommendations of the Le Dain commission whose next report is expected later this year. Drug use is increasing, as the hon. member has shown us by the statistics he quoted, and this is causing concern to regulatory bodies, to federal narcotic agents, to those in our teaching institutions, in our colleges and universities and, most of all perhaps, to parents who in most cases have no idea how to cope with this situation among young people. Most important of all, it is of concern to the young people themselves.
The motion raises the question of how to proceed when attempting to define programs to combat non-medical drug use in ways other than by punitive measures. We are probably moving at this time from an era when drug use was regarded solely as a manifestation of criminal behaviour to one where we try to understand the underlying motives for such use and attempt to help the person involved. In some senses there are parallels to the way in which we ceased to regard alcoholism as deviate behaviour and began to treat it as an illness and alcoholics as sick people in need of help and treatment. There are, I am sure, many lessons we can learn from our experience with alcohol, both positive lessons of useful approaches to take and negative ones of pitfalls to avoid.
The department of health is giving considerable thought, first to the most effective ways in which it can use presently available resources to reduce the dimensions of the problems involved in non-medical drug use and, secondly, to ways in which new resources can be marshalled. Indeed, one of the terms of reference of the commission of inquiry into the non-medical use of drugs was:
To inquire into and recommend with respect to ways or means by which the federal government can act, alone or in its relations with government at other levels, in the reduction of the *dimensions of the problems involved in such use.
Non-Medical Drug Abuse Treatment Centres
So the first point I feel I must make is to caution against precipitate and hasty action before a thorough examination has been made of both treatment programs currently available here in Canada and abroad, and also of the feasibility of using compulsory treatment. In the interim report of the commission of inquiry into the non-medical use of drugs little stress was laid on treatment and other social responses to the phenomenon of non-medical drug use. Rather, the report was primarily concerned with a statement of the issues and applicable principles, with some specific recommendations in the field of research, drug analysis, information and law. In the area of treatment and supportive services the commission made certain recommendations of a general nature but said, more specifically:
In the coming year the commission intends to examine in detail both the concept of psychological dependence and the treatment programs which have evolved, both in Canada and abroad.
Later it said:
The commission recognizes that one of its major tasks in the preparation of its final report will be a thorough examination of the proposals for legislation which would result in compulsory treatment of heavy chronic drug users.
Thus, I wonder if any good purpose would be served in committing ourselves at this juncture to policies which may be invalidated by the further observations of Mr. Gerald Le Dain and the commission.
The concept of treatment means adopting the attitude that we have to concern ourselves with cures for those who have encountered problems as a result of their drug use. This is, sadly, a fact of life today because those who are dependent on drugs and would like to resume a meaningful role in society find many difficulties and little help. We must not let this distort our priorities, however. Our first priority must be to find ways of preventing the problems from arising. Legal sanctions will have an important role to play here, although we must be constantly prepared to examine the relevant acts and regulations so that we are always sure of what we are attempting to control and why.
In the final analysis, however, we have to rely on the good sense of young people to make wise decisions for themselves in their individual attitudes toward drug use. To this end the Department of National Health and Welfare established this summer a drug abuse education unit which is disseminating information both in the form of pamphlets and by speaking to groups. This information is factual in nature and it is hoped that the presentation of such facts to young people will aid them to develop responsible positions on drug use.
However, while most surveys of drug use have studied youthful drug users, we are slowly becoming aware that we cannot concentrate solely on young people. We know, for example, that some of the largest selling drugs in Canada today are minor tranquillizers and we can guess that most of these are prescribed for adults. A recently survey by Mrs. Ruth Cooperstock and Mrs. Sims of the Addiction Research Foundation of Ontario examined the

June 18, 1971
Non-Medical Drug Abuse Treatment Centres extent to which mood-modifying drugs are being prescribed in metropolitan Toronto. They found that 24 per cent of all prescriptions are for mood-modifying drugs

tranquillizers, stimulants and depressants-and that on any given day 7 per cent of the population 15 years of age and older were taking such drugs legally.
A great deal of information was produced and I hope that similar future surveys will give us deeper insights into this largely unknown area of adult drug use. How many of these people for whom such drugs are being prescribed are finding difficulties with their use? How many are building up tolerance and finding ways and means to increase the dose above that stated by their physician? How many are anxious to cut down on their use but don't know how to do it or where to turn for help? We need to get information to adults to help those who have such problems and to help others avoid them.
Adults need information too, not only to help them assess their own drug problems but to help them understand why their own children might turn to drugs in response to the many stresses of modern life. Again, teachers need information if they are to discuss drugs and drug problems with any degree of credibility with young people of some sophistication in this area. Not only the lay public needs information, however. Many medical practitioners are unaware of the dangers of overprescribing these potent drugs; many hospitals are unable to cope with emergencies arising from drug abuse. Thus, two grants of $15,000 were given to the Canadian Hospital Association to assist in planning and implementing a symposium which was held in February in Montreal. At this symposium those who have learned about drug problems the hard way, by practical experience, passed on to those who have yet to face such crises the benefit of their experience and expertise.
The drug scene is, however, not static. New groups are turning to drugs for new reasons. Research is constantly giving us new insights into the mode of action of drugs and the potential hazards of drug use. Without doubt, the number of different mood-modifying drugs will continue to grow. Information dissemination must, therefore, be the handmaiden of research and data retrieval. Thus, the Department of National Health and Welfare made another move in recent weeks with the appointment of a co-ordinator to oversee the information and research programs of the department. He will make available funds to suitable applicants for research into many of the vexing questions that have to be answered if we are to make rational judgments on drug use. He will himself suggest areas of priority for research if suitable programs are not forthcoming. The information which results from these research programs and from research elsewhere in the world will then be processed and made available in forms suitable for various client groups such as educators, parents, young people, medical and paramedical practioners.
This, briefly, is what is already being done to help check and slow down the move toward wider non-medical use of mood-modifying drugs. The problem still remains, however, that we already have casualties in our society
as a result of drug use and we can anticipate that their numbers will increase unless preventive measures begin soon to show an effect on general, over-all use. Without being pessimistic, I cannot see that we have yet found the preventive measures which will have a noticeable affect on non-medical drug use. The latest survey of student drug use in metropolitan Toronto indicates a continued and sharp increase in drug use of a number of types. I am sure that you have all read reports of this survey-virtually a tripling of the number of students using marijuana, LSD and opiates during the past two years. Obviously, we still have cause for concern; obviously, we must continue and intensify our efforts to combat the problem.
Let us, however, keep a sense of perspective. Most people who use alcohol are able to control that use and only a minority, albeit a sizeable minority, become deeply involved and find their use of alcohol to be uncontrollable. We appear to have a similar situation with drug use. We must be careful not to move from the old simplification of treating all drugs use as criminal delinquent behavior to a new one of assuming that all drug use is symptomatic of serious underlying emotional and mental disorders.
It is becoming fashionable to talk of drugs as "the symptom" and not "the problem", so fashionable that it is becoming almost a cliche. We have to learn, rather, to treat the drug user as an individual and to understand that different drugs have differing degrees of hazard. The young person who tries marijuana once is probably not in need of any treatment of the kind proposed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta, and it would be useless to try to force him into an institutional setting to be treated for a condition which does not exist. On the other hand, a minority of marijuana users are finding problems with the drug. They find themselves unable to cope efficiently with their studies or work, and they find themselves being increasingly dependent on the drug whenever stressful situations arise. They may want help but do not know where to find it, just as many tobacco smokers want help but do not know where to go for it. I suggest that such people need a very different kind of treatment from the treatment of a heavy, chronic heroin or speed user.
Much drug use appears to be attribuable to boredom, to peer group pressures, to frustration with our society and its institutions and, perhaps most commonly, merely to a desire for experience. We cannot, therefore, view all drug use as necessarily demanding treatment. We cannot, furthermore, view the drug problem as one problem requiring one approach merely because we have the common denominator of the drug. We must, rather, learn to see it as a human problem, defined by the motivations, personalities and behaviour of people as individuals. Dr. Helen Nowlis, author of "Drugs on the College Campus" and a long-time researcher in the field argues in this way:
There are two separate drug problems. One has to do with drugs as pharmacological substances and the other has to do with people, physiologically, psychologically, socially and philosophically defined, people who use drugs, who have attitudes opinions, and beliefs about drugs and make judgments about

June 18, 1971

drugs, drug use and drug users. Much of our difficulty has arisen because of failure to separate the two problems.
We must explore, therefore, a number of levels of approach to deal with a number of different types of people. The hon. member's motion refers to that minority of drug users who can be defined as chronic users. Such people may need the long-term, live-in type of facility which can help them not only to overcome their physical and/or psychological dependency on drugs but which can also help them to understand their own motivation for resorting to the drug whenever problems appear in this lives. Facilities of this kind already exist, mainly of course in the United States where the problem of chronic drug use has so far reached much larger proportions than it has here. Facilities such as Project Ossington in Toronto, as Daytop Village and Odyssey House in New York, and Synanon in California have had much experience and can teach us a great deal.
One lesson is, I think, that we must not be bureaucratic and limited in our approach, but must be prepared to be sufficiently flexible so that institutions can change with changing social conditions. We have to accept that many of the institutions can change with changing social conditions. We have to accept that many of the institutions we will be called upon the support will be innovative and will be hard to judge and assess by more conventional yardsticks. Often, a treatment facility will depend heavily on the personality, charm or charisma of one person. If this person is able to get results we should be prepared to support him even though he may not conform to our bureaucracy as well as more "establishment" organizations.
Another lesson is that we can only help those who want to be helped. All the successful projects are based on this premise. Often, the prospective applicant is required to call the organization several times before being allowed to enter the program. Some are tired of the life they are leading and of their slavery to drugs, others apply as a condition of probation by the courts. We must be careful, too, not to set up compulsory treatment centres merely as a ruse to remove what we perceive to be undesirable people from society.
Even then, given the motivation on the part of the drug user and the availability of suitable long-term facilities, we would still have to face the problem of the re-entry phase. Many young people who have become deeply involved with drugs have done so in their late teens at a particularly crucial time of their lives. They are just not equipped, educationally or vocationally, to get back into society. We have to look, therefore, to training or retraining as an integral part of any treatment scheme.
The questions of where drug treatment programs should be located and how they should be developed have also to be answered. Should we form highly specialized drug treatment centres which are also responsible for research and clinical evaluation, or should we, rather,
Non-Medical Drug Abuse Treatment Centres allow treatment facilities to grow up where they are needed as grassroots movements and then give financial and other support as necessary? The latter approach has, I think, much merit if we are anxious to avoid bureaucratic, inflexible organizations unable to change and innovate in response to changing social conditions and drug use patterns.
In summary, therefore, I have three points to make. First, we must be careful not to create a number of new institutions which lack effectiveness because of the inflexibility and inability to change with changing conditions. Second, we need in-depth studies of what is already available before proceeding, and since we already have a commission of inquiry working in this area it would be premature to act before their final report is tabled. Third, we must realize that treatment may only supply an answer for a small segment of the drug using population, those involved in heavy, chronic use. The great majority of young people will need factual information to help them make wise decisions and also the opportunity for meaningful positive alternatives so that they have better things to occupy them than resorting to drug use.

subsubtopic: CENTRES TO DEAL WITH NON-MEDICAL DRUG ABUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Goode) for bringing forward this motion. I suggest it is very timely and I am surprised that it would not be accepted by the government without question. It is very easy for backbenchers to present forward-looking proposals in an attempt to deal with social changes, but surely the government has a responsibility in this regard. This kind of motion is indicative of practical solutions to a major problem in our changing social climate, particularly among our young people. The government should at least consider such motions and agree to refer them to a committee for further study.
The idea of establishing drug centres across Canada to co-ordinate treatment and the supply of information in various regions is one that deserves the support of all Canadians. The two hon. members who have spoken drew a parallel in respect of alcohol, smoking and drug use, but they did not refer to the social implications. I do not remember when smoking became a fad, but I do remember when the use of alcohol was considered to be a social stigma. No one could drink legally except for medicinal purposes.
In those days a doctor would make out a prescription and the individual would walk across the street and purchase a bottle of alcohol. Today a number of addicts go to the doctor, obtain a prescription and then walk across the street to the drug store to have it filled. Many people in the professions and in business are using drugs today. They are affluent individuals and can afford to purchase drugs. This is similar to the purchase of alcohol earlier and apparently it does not raise the eyebrows of people who are aware of our social climate.
It was pointed out by the Le Dain commission that even heroin is not a bad drug when used under certain condi-

June 18, 1971
Non-Medical Drug Abuse Treatment Centres tions. I consider this to be one of the worst drugs, but when a doctor prescribes its use individuals can use it over long periods of time without any serious mental or physical difficulty. I suggest there is a problem in the use of drugs similar to the problem which can be created by the use of alcohol. Many people when considering the use of drugs do not realize that young people might like to use them. These young people do not feel there is anything wrong with drug use. The use of alcohol can be just as serious.

speechtext: I beg your pardon?

subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF REGIONAL TREATMENT
subsubtopic: CENTRES TO DEAL WITH NON-MEDICAL DRUG ABUSE
speechtext:
The hon. member's comment proves my point. People no longer believe the use of alcohol is bad, but if you take a large concentration of alcohol into your system it will prove fatal. I think it is fatal to have a 3 per cent blood-alcohol content. The hon. member is surprised by this, but let me suggest that the people of our society have decided they like to drink. One would not think of inviting half a dozen neighbours in for the evemng and serve them tea. I suggest if you did this your neighbours would not come back a second time. It would also indicate that you had never been to their homes, because then you would know the normal pattern is to serve alcoholic beverages.
Mr. O'Leary of the United States believes you can produce an acceptable social climate by the use of LSD. I do not accept that theory. If you produce that kind of effect through the use of hallucinogenic drugs you are in trouble.
We know that most people who experiment with drugs try marijuana. I believe it would be very difficult for anyone to provide medical evidence to indicate that marijuana is any more serious than cigarettes or alcohol. It probably does not produce any bad effect unless one takes too much of it. Anyone who has studied the problems of emphysema or any other lung disease will be aware that anything put into the lungs other than clean air is bad for the lungs. I suggest, however, that marijuana probably is not much worse than any of the social drugs almost everyone uses. It certainly is not any worse than tobacco or alcohol. We regulate those products. The government inspects tobacco.
We are aware of what is happening in many areas. In my own area I have spoken to people who over a long period of time have used marijuana and, I believe, other drugs as well. They indicate they would consider themselves crazy to use the marijuana sold in that area because it is laced with half a dozen impurities. One of the impurities which has been turned up in much of the marijuana used today is strychnine. I do not think anyone would suggest that strychnine is in any form a social drug. We say in a social sense that drugs which are bad cannot be allowed, and therefore we do not do anything about the situation.
I believe 40 per cent or 50 per cent of the people in our society use drugs, although not in the sense the hon.
member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta indicated. These people use aspirin, sleeping tablets, wake-up tablets and all sorts of drugs, some of which they know the purpose of and others they do not. There are drugs to sleep and to wake up. Some of them are not even prescribed drugs. So we have developed a social acceptance of some drugs. Fortunately, those drugs usually are controlled as to impurities. However, we allow young people of seven, eight, and nine years of age to buy marijuana simply because we say the sale of it is illegal and does not exist. Since we say it does not exist, obviously we cannot have inspectors check it for impurities.
I suggest that if we had treatment centres as envisaged in this motion they would be able to find out one simple thing. I am sure they would find that many people who go to hospital as a result of a bad trip or an overdose of drugs find that the potency of these drugs is different from time to time and they really do not know what is the proper usage of the drug they have taken.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me society should soon make up its mind. Prohibition is no good; it does not work. Control may work. However, we have not tried control. Other countries have. In England, if a person should be addicted to cocaine, heroin or any of the so-called hard drugs he can register as an addict and obtain a supply of the drug. The price is reasonable. In conjunction with any kind of drug, here we have the criminal element because a lot of money can be made in its distribution.
If we had treatment centres, I suggest that when the medical evidence is provided by them we would find that the impurities and additives which are being passed around in the trade are so dangerous that it is absolutely necessary that they be controlled. The first thing that is necessary in order to control this situation is to have a social sense of the problem. There were some people who did not like to drink prior to prohibition days.
I for one expect many people drank during the prohibition period who had never taken a drink before and probably have never taken a drink since. They probably drank during prohibition because it was illegal and this added an additional kick to whatever kick they received from alcohol. It was stupid even to consider prohibition. One reason it was stupid is that it is not very difficult to make moonshine. It is not very difficult to make a still and develop alcohol. In respect of the hallucinogenic drugs now being used, I am told that children who take chemistry in high school can go in their own basement and with $5 worth of equipment can turn out some kind of hallucinogenic drugs, impurities and all. If this is so, the parents had better not say that their kids do not use drugs. They had better not say it is only everybody else's kids who use drugs. They should consider the possibility that their children may be using drugs. If they look at the situation fairly and squarely they should suggest that Parliament get busy and bring in controls that would at least protect their children against the deaths now being suffered in many instances not so much because of the drug but, rather the impurities in it.
I congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta on introducing this subject. I commend his

June 18, 1971

motion to his government. I suggest that probably more good ideas are emitted from the backbenches of all parties in this House than from the frontbenches. I believe it would behoove Parliament in general to have a better way of accepting a proposition such as this, to which I am sure no person would object unless they believe the health and development of our young people are not worth the expense of establishing a large number of treatment centres that would provide the population with control and the young people with the assistance they so desperately need.
Mr. Speaker, drugs are probably with us to stay. It is not good enough to say it was not so in father's day and therefore we do not have to consider the problem today. It is wise to look at it and at some of the propositions being put forward by young people. If this is done and receives the kind of publicity and support it should by organizations concerned in this field, then I am very hopeful that within a year or so we will see this kind of centre being established throughout Canada for our young people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Isabelle (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF REGIONAL TREATMENT
subsubtopic: CENTRES TO DEAL WITH NON-MEDICAL DRUG ABUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join those of my colleagues who have congratulated the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Goode) for the very good motion he presented to the House. And, like the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), I want to tell him that good ideas sometimes come from those who do not have the opportunity to be heard as often as others in the House. He may rest assured, however, that what he has said in his motion will be borne in mind by the Department of National Health and Welfare, with regard to the non-medical use of medicines and drugs.
We have heard today a kind of parallel or confrontation-if I may use these terms-on what is or should be the use of alcoholic beverages compared to the non-medical use of drugs. It would be interesting, I believe, to have a debate some day on this important issue which, in my view, as has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Timiskaming, will be with us for a long time.
It is true, however, that according to the motion of our friend from Burnaby-Richmond-Delta, treatment is a solution to the drug problem. In my opinion, this is only partially true, as it would solve only a small part of the problem caused by drugs in Canada.
If we felt that all young people guilty of drug abuse should undergo medical treatment, we would have found a medical solution to boredom, frustration, mental illness as well as to existing physical and affective problems. However, drug abuse may, to a certain extent, be checked by treatment, and we are already working on that. We have considered the following: intervention at the time of the crisis caused by abusive use of certain drugs for non medical purposes and long term rehabilitation.
Non-Medical Drug Abuse Treatment Centres
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is extremely important that we vary the treatment approach for these sick people.
The first one requires immediate medical attention for physical and emotional troubles. There are in Canada centres for the care of critical cases, though they are not in sufficient number-I do not doubt it-since they have been existing only for six years. They have generally beenn established through the initiative of young people, with very limited financial support drawn mainly from local community funds.
Ordinarily, they are free, although a vrey small fee might be asked. This is one of the main features of these centres, especially since they attend, partially at least, to young people on the move who have very little money. In these centres, the atmosphere is quite relaxed, which seems necessary for the type of work that is done there. Along with the youths who are to be found in the centres, there is always voluntary professional personnel available on call. Such personnel may include health officials, doctors, lawyers, psychiatrists, and many others.
It is important to understand that acute reactions to drugs are not the only cases treated in these centres. Other types of medical services are provided, in particular for venereal diseases, hepatitis-a common illness among those who travel extensively-torn skin from walking barefoot as well as fractures.
Some centres are helping people by distributing clothes, vitamins and contraceptives, and by giving advice, for instance, on locally available jobs and by giving legal advice and information on birth control. For example, during the summer of 1970, drug abuse cases ranked only eighth among all cases treated in a clinic in Ottawa.
People often ask why treatment centres should be established in emergency cases when there are hospitals. Unfortunately, the problems of chronic drug use cannot always be solved in general hospitals. For instance, you always have to wait a long time before being admitted into emergency rooms, but drugs effects must be treated without delay.
Moreover, hospitalization cards and some identification are required in hospitals. For one reason or another, many young people do not carry them around. One must nevertheless admit that some hospitals do change their emergency services in order to face problems such as these.
Even the atmosphere of efficiency which normally exists in a hospital becomes a problem in itself since it appears as something altogether unknown to these young people who come in to be treated for negative reactions to drugs. They may easily mistake reality for the confused images which they feel and see when they are under the influence of drugs and this is why, as I said earlier, control centers in critical cases insist on creating an atmosphere of relative relaxation which is vital.
Negative reactions to drugs may get to be dangerous and this is why an effort should be made to bring those people under the influence of drugs back to reality, or to use a familiar phrase, to bring them back to earth. This

June 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Benson
can be achieved, generally, by following two methods: either by administering chimiotherapy, either through the use of tranquilizers or by talking with the patient. Most people working in this field seem to prefer the latter method, which involves personal, intense, warm communication between the patient and the social worker. Usually, hospital personnel do not have time to engage in this kind of therapy in a large hospital.
A significant part of the staff in treatment centres works on a voluntary basis so that salaries are not a major cost component. This permits the hiring of large staffs which help ensure that any person applying to these centres receives immediate help. Usually, people working in these centres can deal with most bad experiences with drugs by talking with the patient, which does not seem to require very sophisticated professional training. This way, the professional staff can concentate on more difficult cases and have more time to study specific cases that should be referred to other institutions. These centres therefore offer a most useful service and their operating costs are small. The staff of most of these centres seem to take their responsibilities very seriously and it is extremely useful to the community.
However, before taking decisions, we must study what is already available in order to establish the best possible programs. Among the services which can be considered are the following: the Youth Centre in Montreal, the Insight-Drug Aid in Fredericton, the Toronto Free Youth Clinic, Digger House in Halifax, Cool Aid in Vancouver. Those are but a few examples. Many others should be studied, and we have the impression that our young people should play an important role in their development, which they will undoubtedly do.

That this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government.
He said: This is an important and historic occasion. It is the birthday of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
